newsitem.title: UK: BoE report to keep hard line on inflation.
newsitem.headline: BoE report to keep hard line on inflation.

text.p: A surprise British interest rate rise last week will take some, but not all, of the sting out of the Bank of England's quarterly inflation report, analysts said on Monday.
The report, due on Wednesday, is unlikely radically to change the Bank's view that inflation is set to miss the government's 2.5 percent target over the medium term.
Higher interest rates and the effective monetary tightening caused by a stronger pound may keep a lid on any build-up of price pressures next year, analysts said.
But with high street spending still rising and GDP statistics showing above-trend growth, the risks are clear.

"The report may show some deterioration in short-term prospects, but looking further ahead, both higher base rates and the firmer currency are likely to result in a more sanguine tone," said Philip Shaw, group economist at Union Plc.

Sterling has risen more than eight percent since early August, when the Bank's last inflation report was published. Last week, the pound got another leg up after Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke stunned the markets with a quarter-point rate rise, taking base rates to six percent.
An old rule of thumb in the markets is that a four percent currency appreciation is equivalent to a one percentage point increase in official short-term rates.
Even if that is overstating the case, the pound's eight percent leap will inevitably start to hit export activity and cut import prices -- both likely to keep the lid on inflation.
Shaw said the report would say the government's target of 2.5 percent for underlying inflation is more likely than not to be met in the medium term, a distinct softening of tone.

In its last report, the Bank said it expected RPIX, the underlying inflation measure that excludes mortgage interest payments, to fall until mid-1997 and then rise to a little above its target a year later.

Other analysts were less confident the Bank would temper its line. "Sterling has appreciated quite strongly but the Bank will say that has been offset by stronger-than-expected growth," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Preliminary data showed GDP growth of 0.8 percent in the third quarter. That puts annualised growth at 3.2 percent, well above the so-called sustainable rate, generally seen to be around 2.5 percent. "Given that the recovery is based around domestic consumer spending, a rate rise may not have much effect," Barr said.

Tighter monetary policy will mute investment and should keep the pound strong. Both factors will hurt manufacturing industry, the area of the economy that needs most help. Meanwhile, buoyant consumers may continue spending regardless, particularly since last week's rate rise did not prompt mortgage lenders to raise their rates.
Barr expects the Bank to say the inflation target will be missed in two years time if rates are left unchanged.
